description: Table 2 is a single rendered data table (no plot, no micrograph). It reports empirical linear elemental coefficients for austenite: A^LP describing the lattice-parameter dependence, in 10⁻³ nm wt.%⁻¹ with bracketed values in 10⁻³ nm at.%⁻¹, and A^SFE describing the stacking-fault-energy dependence, in mJ m⁻² wt.%⁻¹ (the bracketed unit printed in that header reads [10⁻³ nm at.%⁻¹], which is inconsistent with the column's own units and appears to be a typographic error). The table has four columns — Element; A^LP (this study); A^LP "From Dyson and Holmes [16]"; A^SFE — and exactly two rows, Si and Al. Si: A^LP = −0.018 [−0.009], Dyson–Holmes ≈0 [≈0], A^SFE = −2.6 [−1.3]. Al: A^LP = 0.582 [0.289], Dyson–Holmes 0.56 [0.28], A^SFE = 4.9 [2.5]. No uncertainties are printed. The table's role is to show that the newly determined Si and Al lattice-parameter coefficients agree closely with the Dyson and Holmes values, and that Si lowers while Al raises the austenite SFE.

observations.observation: The table contains exactly two data rows, labelled Si and Al, and four columns (Element; A^LP this study; A^LP from Dyson and Holmes [16]; A^SFE).
For Si the lattice-parameter coefficient is printed as −0.018 in 10⁻³ nm wt.%⁻¹, bracketed [−0.009] in 10⁻³ nm at.%⁻¹.
For Al the lattice-parameter coefficient is printed as 0.582 in 10⁻³ nm wt.%⁻¹, bracketed [0.289] in 10⁻³ nm at.%⁻¹.
The literature comparison column attributed to Dyson and Holmes [16] lists ≈0 [≈0] for Si and 0.56 [0.28] for Al in 10⁻³ nm wt.%⁻¹.
The SFE coefficient A^SFE is printed as −2.6 [−1.3] for Si and 4.9 [2.5] for Al, in mJ m⁻² wt.%⁻¹.
The bracketed unit in the A^SFE column header is printed as [10⁻³ nm at.%⁻¹], which does not match the mJ m⁻² wt.%⁻¹ units of that column; the figure itself does not resolve the inconsistency.
The caption states the table gives empirical Si and Al linear elemental coefficients for austenite lattice parameter and SFE.
The citing text states the calculated A^LP for Si and Al are −0.018 and 0.582 ×10⁻³ nm wt.%⁻¹ respectively and that these agree well with Dyson and Holmes [16].
The citing text states the empirical SFE relation has the form SFE = Σ A_i^SFE x_i with x_i the wt.% of element i in austenite and A_i^SFE in mJ m⁻² wt.%⁻¹.
The citing text states A_Si^SFE values in the high-Mn steel literature vary from 1 to 3.5 mJ m⁻² wt.%⁻¹ and are in good agreement with the −2.6 mJ m⁻² wt.%⁻¹ found in this study (Table 2).
The citing text states thermochemical modeling predicts A_Al^SFE ≈ 5.2 mJ m⁻² wt.%⁻¹, in very good agreement with the 4.9 mJ m⁻² wt.%⁻¹ of this study (Table 2).

The citing text reports other literature A_Al^SFE values for comparison: ≈6.4 mJ m⁻² wt.%⁻¹ (Jeong et al. [28]), 6.9 mJ m⁻² wt.%⁻¹ estimated in this study after accounting for partial dislocation strain fields, and 11.3 mJ m⁻² wt.%⁻¹ (Kim et al. [23]).
No experimental uncertainty, standard deviation or error value is printed for any coefficient in the table.

subfigures.description: Two-row, four-column data table of empirical linear coefficients for austenite. Rows: Si (A^LP = −0.018 [−0.009]; Dyson and Holmes [16] ≈0 [≈0]; A^SFE = −2.6 [−1.3]) and Al (A^LP = 0.582 [0.289]; Dyson and Holmes 0.56 [0.28]; A^SFE = 4.9 [2.5]). All coefficients are legible; no error bars or uncertainties are given.
